label: Problem set 2
title: Problem set 2: Reflection, refraction, diffraction and polarisation
summary: Practice the wave theory of Lesson 2: the law of reflection, Snell’s law, the change of speed and wavelength in a medium, and the meaning of diffraction, interference and polarisation.

intro.text: This set practises the behaviour of light as a wave: how it reflects, how it bends on entering a new medium, and what diffraction, interference and polarisation tell us. The key equation is Snell’s law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
Remember the definition of refractive index, n = c / v, where v is the speed of light in the medium. On entering a denser medium the light slows down, so it bends towards the normal.

sections.title: Reflection, refraction and wave phenomena
sections.summary: Apply the law of reflection and Snell’s law, and reason about diffraction, interference and polarisation.
keyPoints: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.
Snell’s law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
Refractive index n = c / v; entering a denser medium slows the light and bends it towards the normal.
Diffraction, interference and polarisation are all wave effects.

blocks.text: Reflection keeps the speed and simply turns the ray. Refraction is more interesting: the speed changes, and because the frequency is fixed by the source, the wavelength must change too. The steeper the change of speed, the more the ray bends.

blocks.caption: Snell’s law and the refractive index

blocks.text: Keep the frequency fixed when light enters a medium. The frequency is set by the source and never changes; what changes is the speed and, with it, the wavelength.

blocks.title: Refraction at an air–water surface
blocks.given: Light passes from air (n = 1.00) into water (n = 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 35°. Find the angle of refraction.
blocks.result: The ray bends towards the normal and enters the water at about 26°.

blocks.title: A quick check
blocks.body: When the second medium is denser (n₂ > n₁), the refracted ray is always closer to the normal than the incident ray. If your answer comes out larger than the incident angle, something has gone wrong.

questions.question: Why does a pencil look bent where it enters a glass of water?
options: light slows down and changes direction at the surface
light is absorbed by the water
the water emits its own light
questions.explanation: Light travels more slowly in water than in air, so at the surface it changes direction: refraction. Your eye traces the bent ray back in a straight line, so the pencil looks kinked.

questions.question: The angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence.
questions.explanation: This is the law of reflection, with both angles measured from the normal to the surface. It holds for every smooth surface.

questions.question: Light enters glass (n = 1.50) from air (n = 1.00) at an angle of incidence of 40°. Find the angle of refraction, in degrees.
questions.explanation: sin θ₂ = (1.00/1.50) sin 40° = 0.429, so θ₂ = sin⁻¹(0.429) = 25.6°. The ray bends towards the normal.

questions.question: A light wave of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz enters a medium in which its speed is 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Find its wavelength in the medium, in metres.
questions.explanation: The frequency is unchanged, so λ = v / f = (2.0 × 10⁸) / (5.0 × 10¹⁴) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.

questions.question: Diffraction is clearest when:
options: the gap is much wider than the wavelength
the gap is comparable in size to the wavelength
there is no gap at all
questions.explanation: Waves spread noticeably when they pass through an opening about the same size as their wavelength. Through a very wide gap the spreading is negligible.

questions.question: Interference and diffraction are evidence that light behaves as a wave.
questions.explanation: Both arise from the adding and cancelling of overlapping waves, and both are seen with light. They are among the strongest evidence for the wave theory.

questions.question: Which of these are wave phenomena? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Reflection, polarisation and diffraction are all described by the wave picture. The photoelectric effect belongs to the particle picture.

questions.question: Unpolarised light passes through a single polarising filter. The light that comes out is:
questions.explanation: The filter passes only the component of the electric field along its axis, so the transmitted light oscillates in a single plane. A second filter at right angles would block it entirely.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.50. Find its wavelength inside the glass, in nanometres. (The frequency is unchanged.)
questions.explanation: The speed and wavelength both fall by the factor n, so λ(glass) = 600 / 1.50 = 400 nm. The colour does not change, because the frequency is the same.

questions.question: White light splits into colours through a prism because different colours refract by different amounts.
questions.explanation: The refractive index depends slightly on wavelength, so each colour bends a little differently and the colours separate. This is dispersion.

questions.question: The refractive index n of a medium is defined as:
questions.explanation: The refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in the medium, n = c / v. A larger n means a slower speed and a denser medium.

questions.question: Two loudspeakers play the same steady tone, yet you find quiet spots in the room. The reason is:
options: the waves interfere destructively at some points
the speakers turn each other off
questions.explanation: Where a crest of one wave meets a trough of the other they cancel, giving a quiet point. This destructive interference is a general property of waves, sound and light alike.

questions.question: A wave has a frequency of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find its wavelength in nanometres. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Diffraction is more noticeable when the slit or obstacle is comparable in size to the wavelength.
questions.explanation: Strong diffraction requires the wavelength to be comparable to the size of the opening; if the slit is far larger, diffraction is slight.

questions.question: Which of the following are wave behaviours of light? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Interference, diffraction and polarisation are wave effects. The photoelectric effect shows particle behaviour.
